page_title: Ways to make fake data look meaningful

sources.entry: Ways to make fake data look meaningful

summary.title: Ways to make fake data look meaningful
summary.one_liner: A satirical checklist of tricks for making statistics look more convincing than they are, and why readers should demand raw data and methodology.
takeaways: Withholding raw data, methodology, and caveats makes statistical conclusions harder to challenge, which is why readers should ask for them.
Confidence intervals convey uncertainty; omitting or misstating their confidence level makes results look more certain than they are.
Graphs invite pattern matching, and random data can appear meaningful, so visuals need scrutiny.
The author proposes the response 'raw data or it didn't happen' to demand evidence for impressive analytical claims.
summary.summary: This short essay is written as a tongue-in-cheek list of rules for making data look more meaningful than it is, such as not sharing raw data or methodology, omitting confidence intervals, using lots of graphs, and refusing to challenge your own analysis. It uses a sample A/B testing table to show how a lower confidence level makes the interval look narrower and more impressive. A footnote explains that the binomial proportion interval comes from abba, an open-source split testing calculator. The afterword flips the satire into advice: be skeptical of other people's data and demand raw data and clear methods.
